summary: Describes the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol. A host or router on a non-broadcast multi-access network, such as ATM, can use it to find the addresses needed to reach the next hop toward a destination, often allowing a direct shortcut.

eli5.summary: Like asking a helper for the shortest path across a big building with no hallway signs, so you can go directly instead of through every room.

questions: how do hosts find shortcuts on atm networks
what is a next hop server
subtitle: How a host or router on a non-broadcast network like ATM asks servers for the address of its next hop, so traffic can take a direct shortcut.

tldr.problem: On a non-broadcast, multi-access (NBMA) network such as ATM, ordinary ARP only works inside one logical IP subnet, so traffic between subnets takes extra router hops through the same network.
tldr.mechanism: A source sends an NHRP Resolution Request toward the destination along the routed path. The Next Hop Server that serves the destination replies with the NBMA address of the destination, or of the egress router nearest to it.
tldr.outcome: The source can then reach the next hop directly, for example by opening a connection, instead of crossing intermediate routers. Authentication, caching and loop-avoidance rules keep the exchange safe.

today: RFC 2332 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It points to separate documents for using NHRP between routers for destinations off the NBMA subnetwork, and for the transition from Classical IP and ARP over ATM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) lets a source station, a host or a router, find the internetworking layer address and the NBMA address of a suitable next hop toward a destination. If the destination is attached to the NBMA subnetwork, the next hop is the destination itself. Otherwise it is the egress router from the NBMA subnetwork that is nearest to the destination. A subnetwork can be non-broadcast because it cannot broadcast, such as X.25, or because broadcasting is not feasible, such as a very large SMDS multicast group.

Earlier models used logically independent IP subnets (LISs), where members of a LIS share a network number and mask, and anything outside is reached through a router. ARP-style resolution only resolves the next hop inside the same LIS, so packets between LISs may cross several IP hops inside one NBMA network. NHRP is meant to reduce or eliminate those extra hops, and can be deployed without interfering with existing ARP services. It is intended as a functional superset of the NBMA Address Resolution Protocol (NARP).
sections.eli5: On some networks, you cannot just shout to find a friend. NHRP gives you a way to ask who to call, so you can reach them directly.

sections.title: Clients, Servers and Logical NBMA Subnetworks
sections.content:
A station that answers NHRP Resolution Requests is a Next Hop Server (NHS). A station that asks is a Next Hop Client (NHC). An NHS is always tightly coupled with a routing entity, and each NHS serves a set of destination hosts that may or may not be directly attached to the NBMA subnetwork. The NHS that serves a destination must lie on the routed path to it, which is why egress routers double as NHSs for the destinations behind them.

A physical NBMA subnetwork may be split into several disjoint logical NBMA subnetworks, each a group of hosts and routers with unfiltered connectivity (no closed user groups or address screening). NHRP requests and replies do not cross the border of a NBMA subnetwork, so data traffic into and out of it always passes a router at its border.

An NHS keeps a cache of protocol-to-NBMA address mappings, built from Registration packets, from Resolution Request and Reply packets, or from outside mechanisms such as ARP or configured tables. An NHC also keeps a cache, filled from Resolution Replies, manual configuration or outside means.
sections.eli5: Clients are people asking for directions. Servers are the helpers who know the way. Each helper looks after a group of people and knows where they all sit.

sections.title: How a Resolution Works
sections.content:
When station S wants to reach destination D, it first finds the next hop through normal routing. If its cache already has the answer, it uses it. Otherwise it builds an NHRP Resolution Request holding D's address, its own address and its NBMA addressing information, and sends it toward D. S may also ask for an authoritative answer only.

While waiting, S may drop the data packet, hold it, or forward it along the routed path. The last is the recommended default, since data can flow while the address is resolved. A request for a given destination must not be triggered on every packet.

Each NHS that receives the request checks whether it serves D. If not, it forwards the request to another NHS. If it does, it sends back a positive Resolution Reply marked authoritative. A transit NHS may cache a reply and later answer with non-authoritative information, but NHSs must not answer authoritative requests from cache. If no NHS can answer, or one cannot forward the request, a negative reply (NAK) comes back. A reply may also carry a prefix length so one answer covers all addresses sharing that prefix.
sections.eli5: You ask the nearest helper. If that helper does not know your friend, they pass your question along until the helper who does know answers, and you get a straight route to your friend.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
Every NHRP packet has a Fixed Part of 20 octets, a Mandatory Part that depends on the packet type, and an optional Extensions Part. The fixed header carries the address family (ar$afn), the protocol type, a hop count, the packet size, a standard IP checksum, an extensions offset, a version (1 for NHRP) and the packet type. The hop count works like a TTL: if an NHS would forward a packet whose hop count is zero, it sends back an error indication and drops the packet.

Most mandatory parts have a common header (source and destination protocol address lengths, flags, a 32-bit Request ID) followed by zero or more Client Information Entries (CIEs). Each CIE holds a code, a prefix length, an MTU, a holding time in seconds, a preference, and the client's NBMA address, subaddress and protocol address. The Request ID is copied from request to reply so the sender can match them.

On networks such as SMDS the packet is preceded by LLC/SNAP encapsulation, and ATM can use either LLC/SNAP or no encapsulation on a circuit dedicated to one protocol. Frame Relay and X.25 identify NHRP with an NLPID of 0x0080 and the same SNAP contents.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a standard cover sheet, then a list of who is asking about whom, and finally optional extra notes stapled on the end.

sections.title: Registration, Purge and Error Messages
sections.content:
A client tells its server where it is with an NHRP Registration Request. The server answers with a Registration Reply, which is a NAK if any CIE has a nonzero code. The reply must travel over a direct NBMA connection to the client, which the server sets up if needed. A client must resend registrations often enough to keep them alive, and the recommended interval is one-third of the Holding Time. The Request ID for registrations must be kept in non-volatile memory so a client that crashes and registers again causes no inconsistency. A client can set the Uniqueness bit to claim that its address is unique, and a second such registration is rejected with code 14.

An NHRP Purge Request invalidates cached information, for example when an egress point has changed. A receiver must discard matching entries and must return a Purge Reply, unless the N bit says no reply is wanted. A client can also purge its own registration. After a purge, a station that wants to talk to the destination again should make an authoritative request to avoid stale entries in intermediate NHSs.

An Error Indication reports problems such as an unrecognized extension (code 1), a loop (3), an unreachable protocol address (6), a protocol error (7), an oversize packet (8), an authentication failure (11) or an exceeded hop count (15). An error indication is never generated in response to another error indication.
sections.eli5: Registering is signing the guest book at the front desk. A purge is crossing a name out because the person moved. An error message is a note saying something went wrong with your question.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
Extensions are type-length-value triplets after the mandatory part, ending with a Null TLV. The Compulsory bit decides what happens when a station does not recognize one. If it is clear, the extension can safely be ignored but must be returned unchanged in a reply. If it is set, the responder must return an Unrecognized Extension error. A transit NHS that cannot process a compulsory extension must act only as a forwarding agent. Extensions keep their order, and a given type may appear once unless stated otherwise.

The defined extensions are the Responder Address extension (type 3), the Forward Transit NHS Record (type 4) and Reverse Transit NHS Record (type 5), which list the NHSs a request or reply passed through and help detect loops, the Authentication extension (type 7) and the Vendor-Private extension (type 8), the only one that may appear more than once. Extension types are divided into ranges for NHRP, the ATM Forum, the IETF and experimental use.
sections.eli5: Extras are sticky notes on a letter. If a note is marked must-read and you cannot read it, you must say so. If it is not marked, you can skip it but hand it back.

sections.title: Deployment, Caching and the Domino Effect
sections.content:
NHRP needs a contiguous deployment of NHRP-capable routers along the path, because a router that does not speak NHRP drops the packets and partitions reachability. In that case the client should fall back to the routed path. When a LIS or LAG has two or more NHSs, their resolution databases should be kept in step, and it is recommended to use the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (RFC 2334).

Cache rules differ by role. Source stations must cache replies they are using and incomplete entries so retries reuse the Request ID, and must purge expired entries and entries named in a Purge Request. Transit NHSs may cache only for non-authoritative use and only for the Holding Time. The prefix length must be used with restraint, only when all covered destinations are on the NBMA network or attached to the responder.

Router-to-router use can create a stable routing loop if information used in route selection is lost, for example BGP path vector information, so NHRP should not be used in such cases. The domino effect occurs when a packet triggers a request at every router along the path. NHS implementations must have a mechanism to prevent it, such as triggering requests only from traffic arriving on non-NBMA interfaces.
sections.eli5: All the helpers along the road must know the system, or the question gets lost. They also keep notes for a limited time, and they should not all start asking the same question at once.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
The Authentication extension protects NHRP hop by hop. It holds a Security Parameter Index (SPI), the source address and a keyed hash calculated over the entire NHRP payload with the data field zeroed. The default algorithm is HMAC-MD5-128. Manual keying must be supported, and any Internet standard key management protocol may be used. A packet that fails authentication causes an Authentication Failure error and is discarded.

Because checks happen hop by hop, a chain of trust exists among NHRP entities, and a compromised entity compromises the whole NHRP domain. Without authentication, entities are open to spoofing and to active and passive attacks. There is no encryption in NHRP, and the RFC assumes a standard layer 3 confidentiality mechanism. A rogue host can try to overload the first hop NHS with requests and registrations. With authentication only that first hop is affected, since unauthenticated packets are dropped instead of forwarded.
sections.eli5: Each helper checks a secret stamp on every message from its neighbor. If the stamp is wrong, the message is thrown away. This only works if every helper keeps their stamp secret.

messages.label: Resolution Request

fields.name: ar$afn
fields.desc: Address family of the link layer addresses carried.

fields.name: ar$pro.type
fields.desc: Protocol type of the internetwork layer.

fields.name: ar$pro.snap
fields.desc: SNAP-coded protocol ID when ar$pro.type is 0x0080, otherwise zero.

fields.name: ar$hopcnt
fields.desc: Maximum number of NHSs the packet may traverse.

fields.name: ar$pktsz
fields.desc: Total length of the NHRP packet in octets.

fields.name: ar$chksum
fields.desc: Standard IP checksum over the whole NHRP packet.

fields.name: ar$extoff
fields.desc: Offset of the first extension, or 0 if none.

fields.name: ar$shtl
fields.desc: Type and length of the source NBMA address.

fields.name: ar$sstl
fields.desc: Type and length of the source NBMA subaddress.

items.label: Resolution Request
items.desc: Asks for the next hop NBMA information for a destination.

items.label: Resolution Reply
items.desc: Returns the answer, or a NAK.

items.label: Registration Request
items.desc: A client registers its NBMA information with its server.

items.label: Purge Reply
items.desc: Confirms that the information was purged.

items.label: Error Indication
items.desc: Reports an error to the sender of an NHRP packet.
